The salt spray had long since stained Elias’s knuckles a permanent, rusty orange. For forty years, he had been the sentinel of Blackwood Point, a jagged tooth of granite jutting into the churning Atlantic. His world was reduced to the rhythmic sweep of the Fresnel lens, the groan of the iron gears, and the relentless, indifferent roar of the sea below.

Tonight, the storm was particularly vicious. Rain lashed against the thick glass of the lantern room like handfuls of gravel, threatening to extinguish the light that had guided sailors to safety for over a century. Elias adjusted his oilskin coat, his arthritic knees protesting with every step up the spiral stairs. He checked the fuel gauge. It was low. Too low.

A sharp crack echoed through the tower, louder than the thunder. A branch, torn from the ancient oak on the cliffside, had smashed into the lower gallery. Dust and debris rained down from the ceiling. Elias froze. The structural integrity of the base was compromised. If the foundation cracked, the entire tower could slide into the abyss.
